Each card is a short, self-contained lesson of five to ten minutes. It gives the background on the people and ideas involved, then a tension where two thinkers genuinely disagree, in their own words, quoted and cited. Next comes a question meant for discussion, and last a line I call the moral, unresolved: a plain statement of what is at stake that does not pretend to settle the disagreement. Most of these questions do not have a clean answer. That is the point.

Three goals

Martha Nussbaum’s Cultivating Humanity (1997) argues that a liberal education should develop three abilities. Each card is built toward one of them.

Socratic self-examination

The capacity to question yourself and your own traditions, keeping only the beliefs that hold up under the demand for consistency and justification.

World citizenship

The capacity to see yourself as a human being bound to all other human beings by ties of recognition and concern, not only as a citizen of a local region or group.

Narrative imagination

The ability to imagine what it might be like to be in the shoes of a person different from yourself, and to read that person’s story intelligently.

Martha C. Nussbaum, Cultivating Humanity: A Classical Defense of Reform in Liberal Education (Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1997).
